stories.headline: 2026 NBA buzz: Latest free agency and trade updates
stories.summary: We're tracking deals, trades and buzz across the NBA, including Pelle Larsson getting a long-term extension with the Heat.
stories.body:
NBA free agency has almost reached the end, with several players landing in new homes this offseason.

LeBron James decided to continue his historic career with the Philadelphia 76ers after months of deliberation. The Sixers also traded for Jaylen Brown this summer, turning the franchise into a true contender with two huge moves.

Meanwhile, Giannis Antetokounmpo is headed to South Beach to team up with Bam Adebayo and the Miami Heat, and the Los Angeles Lakers have been sold for the second time in 10 months.

What will happen next during this turbulent offseason?

Check back here for all the latest buzz, news and reactions from our ESPN NBA insiders, with the latest info at the top:

Quick links:

Free agency grades | Trade grades

Trade tracker | Transactions

Depth charts | Trade machine | More

Sept. 18

Pistons, Thompson reach five-year, $155 million extension
Detroit Pistons All-Defensive forward Ausar Thompson has agreed to a five-year, $155 million rookie-scale contract extension with the franchise, sources told ESPN.

Thompson lands the fully guaranteed extension after making first-team All-Defense and finishing third in Defensive Player of the Year voting last season. The 23-year-old averaged 9.9 points, 5.7 rebounds, 3.1 assists and 0.9 blocks in 2025-26 while leading the NBA in steals per game (2.0).

Heat, Larsson agree to four-year, $60 million extension
Miami Heat guard Pelle Larsson has agreed to a new four-year, $60 million contract extension, with a mutual option for the 2030-31 season, Austin Brown and Steven Heumann of CAA Sports told ESPN on Friday.

A second-round find in the 2024 draft, the 6-foot-5 guard avoids restricted free agency next summer and locks in a new deal with a mutual option that fully guarantees $60 million while allowing either side to opt in on 2030.

Jazz, George agree on a five-year, rookie-scale extension
Utah Jazz guard Keyonte George have agreed on a five-year, $157.5 million rookie-scale contract extension with the franchise, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania and Tim MacMahon. George was the No. 16 pick in the 2023 draft and has averaged 17.2 points and 5.3 assists per game in his three seasons with the Jazz.

Sept. 17

Bey, Pelicans agree to three-year extension
New Orleans Pelicans' Saddiq Bey agreed to a three-year, $55.5 million contract extension with the franchise, plus a trade kicker, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Bey averaged a career-high 17.7 points per game last season after missing all of the 2024-25 season with a torn ACL.

Sept. 16

Kings remain interested in Duren
The Sacramento Kings continue to loom in the background of Jalen Duren's restricted free agency with the incumbent Detroit Pistons.

Kings general manager Scott Perry met with Duren for dinner in Miami in early July and has maintained a level of steady interest in the ultimate outcome of Duren's free agency, though a path to acquire Duren this summer remains blocked.

The Pistons declined any legitimate conversation about a Duren sign-and-trade to the Kings for starting center Domantas Sabonis and have maintained a strong stance about their intention to keep Duren.

As ESPN reported earlier this month, the Pistons have a five-year offer in the $35 million per year range on the table, but that hasn't been enough to entice the disgruntled Duren to sign.

His greatest piece of leverage is a risky one -- the $9.6 million qualifying offer that would make him an unrestricted free agent next summer, when Sacramento will have flexibility for the first time in Perry's tenure as general manager. Zach LaVine's $48.9 million contract and De'Andre Hunter's $24.9 million contract both expire, allowing the Kings to generate a max offer for Duren, should he be available.

But that would only be the case if Duren is willing to take a massive one-year paycut and accept the risk of the qualifying offer. Until then, the Kings remain in the background as an interested long-term suitor helping Duren's leverage. -- Anthony Slater

Knicks sign Brown to training camp contract
The New York Knicks are signing Bruce Brown to a training camp contract, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. New York will also have "John Konchar, Drew Eubanks and others enter camp to compete for the final regular season roster," per Charania.

Sept. 15

Shams: NBA Las Vegas expansion plans due Thursday
The NBA and commissioner Adam Silver are in deep expansion conversations with Las Vegas, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania, with the next round of bids due Thursday. Charania also reported that the final round of bids will be due shortly after this round and that his understanding is that the Las Vegas expansion proposal could exceed $10 billion.

The expansion process is ongoing in Seattle as well, per Charania, but hasn't gained as much momentum as Las Vegas currently. Charania expects clarity on votes on both expansion franchises "over the next couple months."

Sept. 14

Sources: Duren feels 'disrespected' in contract talks
The Detroit Pistons are focused on bringing back restricted free agent Jalen Duren, Andscape's Marc Spears said on "NBA Today," but there are feelings to mend.

"They have some optimism, but it's complicated," Spears said. "I just hear that, for Jalen, it's not about money right now. He feels disrespected. ... There's a black cloud going into camp. ... They gotta try to fix it, and I don't know if they can in time."

Kawhi Leonard trade to Toronto officially confirmed

The trade sending Kawhi Leonard to the Toronto Raptors for Gradey Dick, Brandon Ingram and future draft picks was confirmed Monday, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

Taj Gibson officially retires, joins Bulls as assistant coach

Following a 17-year NBA career, Taj Gibson has retired and agreed to return to the Chicago Bulls as an assistant coach under Tiago Splitter, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

Sept. 13

Ballmer and Clippers to comply with NBA punishments
Eleven days after the NBA issued punishments stemming from its investigation into the LA Clippers' dealings with Kawhi Leonard, team owner Steve Ballmer issued a statement saying he and the team would comply with them.

Those punishments include a $30 million fine, yearlong suspensions for Ballmer and president of business operations Gillian Zucker, a six-month suspension for president of basketball operations Lawrence Frank, and five lost first-round picks.

Sept. 10

Justice Department opens criminal inquiry into Clippers' dealings with Leonard
The U.S. Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation into the LA Clippers, The New York Times reported Thursday evening, looking at how the team allegedly arranged secret sponsorship contracts for Leonard.

The probe is being conducted by the U.S. attorney's office in Brooklyn, New York.

Sept. 8

Pelicans trade Hawkins to Grizzlies in four-player deal
The New Orleans Pelicans have traded Jordan Hawkins, Micah Peavy, a future second-round pick and a future second-round pick swap to the Memphis Grizzlies for AJ Johnson and Taj Gibson, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania on Tuesday.

The trade clears roster space for the Pelicans, frees up salary flexibility to sign Bennedict Mathurin to a two-year, $16 million deal, and allows the team to have a look at a young player in Johnson, who was the No. 21 pick in the 2023 NBA draft. Hawkins, a lottery pick at No. 14 in the same draft, now gets dealt by his team prior to his fourth season.

Sept. 4

Ben Simmons signs with Kings on one-year deal
Three-time All-Star Ben Simmons has agreed to a one-year, $3.5 million deal with the Sacramento Kings, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. The deal marks a return to the NBA for Simmons, who sat out the 2025-26 season. Simmons was the No. 1 pick in the 2016 NBA draft.

Sept. 3

Windhorst: Steve Ballmer 'very' angry after NBA penalty
ESPN's Brian Windhorst reported that LA Clippers owner Steve Ballmer is 'very angry' after the penalties handed down to the franchise by the NBA on Sept. 2.

"When you're worth $150 billion and you're angry, and he's very clearly angry, you can't advise him, you can't talk to him," Windhorst said on Get Up. "I'd be stunned if his lawyers didn't advise him, as Shams [Charania] said, to make a plea deal because he should've made a please deal."

Read more: NBA punishes Clippers after Kawhi investigation: Top questions​

Thompson, Rockets agree to five-year contract extension
The Houston Rockets and Amen Thompson have agreed to a five-year, $208 million rookie-scale contract extension, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania The deal includes a 10% trade kicker.

Sept. 2

NBA insiders answer the biggest questions on NBA's Clippers investigation
After the NBA released the findings of its yearlong investigation into allegations that the LA Clippers circumvented the salary cap in order to funnel money to Kawhi Leonard, ESPN NBA insiders Baxter Holmes, Brian Windhorst, Ramona Shelburne and Bobby Marks examined the report, the massive punishments the NBA leveled and how all of it could impact this season -- and beyond.

The punishment was compounded by the Clippers being previous offenders during Steve Ballmer's tenure as owner. They were fined $250,000 for a similar accusation involving DeAndre Jordan in 2015. There also was a 2019 investigation into Leonard's signing in which the Clippers were cleared of wrongdoing but subsequently warned and put through a seminar to remind them of the rules.
This penalty is indeed harsh, but it could have been worse.

In the case of Joe Smith and the Minnesota Timberwolves in 2000, his contract was voided and his Bird rights were vacated.

Leonard will have to write a sizable check -- $700,000 -- but he will not be suspended, and his contract and Bird rights remain unaffected.

The Clippers and the Toronto Raptors will be allowed to move forward in their trade process, one league source said. If the trade moves forward, LA will acquire two first-round picks in the deal. -- Windhorst

Read the full story here.

Charania: NBA rules on Kawhi Leonard-Aspiration investigation
Sources told ESPN's Shams Charania reported that, after a year-long probe into Kawhi Leonard-Aspiration connection, the NBA has stripped the LA Clippers of five first-round picks and issued a $30 million fine to owner Steve Ballmer, as well as suspended Ballmer, Lawrence Frank and Gillian Zucker.

On top of that, Leonard will have to pay $700,000 in restitution for improper benefits by the franchise for his uncle and former business representative, Dennis Robertson. Leonard will not be suspended but Robertson is banned by the NBA from all business dealings.

SEC requesting information from Daktronics regarding Clippers probe
The Securities and Exchange Commission is seeking information from Daktronics, the company that designed the LA Clippers' videoboard inside the Intuit Dome, related to Kawhi Leonard, a company executive said Wednesday.

"Let me now briefly address a matter that has been in the media concerning the NBA's investigation of Kawhi Leonard and the Clippers in connection with the league's collective bargaining agreement that many of you may have heard about," chief financial officer Howard Atkins said on Daktronics' quarterly earnings call.

"As you might expect, we have received requests for information from the NBA. Additionally, the Securities and Exchange Commission is seeking information from us concerning the company and Mr. Leonard. "We take these requests seriously and are cooperating. At this point, out of respect for the respective processes, we will not be providing further comment."

A spokesperson for the SEC declined to comment.

Podcaster Pablo Torre reported last month that Daktronics had an undisclosed sponsorship agreement allegedly worth millions of dollars with Leonard.

Torre interviewed someone identified as an "anonymous high-level source under contract for Intuit Dome" who alleged that the sponsorship deal "was 1,000% a way to circumvent the salary cap. It was funneling money from the Clippers through Daktronics back to Kawhi."

The NBA launched its investigation into the Clippers and Leonard last September after numerous podcasts from Torre, who cited internal documents that showed that Clippers owner Steve Ballmer invested $50 million in Aspiration, a now-defunct green banking company, through his personal LLC in September 2021.

That month, the Clippers signed a 23-year, $300 million deal with Aspiration, making the company the "first founding partner" of the Intuit Dome.

Six months later, Aspiration signed its $28 million endorsement deal with Leonard.

An unnamed employee who purportedly worked for the banking company told Torre that Leonard's sponsorship deal "was to circumvent the salary cap."

The Clippers have repeatedly denied that they funneled money through Aspiration to compensate Leonard.

On Aug. 17, ESPN reported that the NBA has found no evidence showing Ballmer funneled money through team sponsors to pay Leonard in order to circumvent the salary cap, per three people with knowledge of recent discussions between the two sides. -- Baxter Holmes

Sept. 1

Windhorst: Sabonis hired new agent this summer, could want out of Sacramento

On the Sept. 1 episode of "The Hoop Collective," ESPN's Brian Windhorst discussed what Domantas Sabonis hiring a new agent this summer could mean for his future with the Sacramento Kings.

Windhorst on Sabonis hiring a new agent: " I do think it's somewhat interesting that he changed agents this offseason. He hired Aaron Mintz of CAA. Steve Heumann and that group. One of the top executives at CAA. This last year, Mintz and his group executed the trade for Trae Young away from Atlanta, executed the trade for Walker Kessler away from the [Jazz]. Domantas Sabonis just hired him.

"At the risk of ... parodying myself from the season, why would he do that?"

Aug. 29

Latest on Curry's next deal decision

The window for Stephen Curry to sign an extension has officially opened.

The four-time champion and two-time MVP is now eligible (through June 30) to sign a two-year, $136.7 million extension. If he signs, Curry will become the first player in NBA history to rack up more than $600 million in on-court earnings.

A new contract for Curry will have important financial implications for Golden State. With Curry, Draymond Green and Jimmy Butler III able to become free agents after the 2026-27 season, Golden State could have significant cap space to reshape its roster.

Though many were surprised the Hornets would not run it back after they won 44 games and came within one play-in win of snapping a playoff drought that dates to 2016, Peterson said he saw something in the turnaround that helped him make this trade with confidence.

Peterson said that when the Hornets were one of the hottest teams in the league after Jan. 2, he liked enough of what he saw from Brandon Miller and Kon Knueppel to believe that they can keep the Hornets' offense buzzing without Ball.

"Everyone would agree, [Miller's] an enormous talent," Peterson said. "He showed a tremendous amount of growth last season, battling through an injury, but was able to continue to persevere and again, help us achieve some results that made our fanbase and us very, very proud. His willingness to continue to fight through some pain and play through some injuries. Of course, everyone knows he's skilled and athletic and he has a true desire to win and continue to get better. So could not be more excited to be going into next season with Brandon Miller on our squad."

Miller played in 65 games and averaged 20.2 points, 4.9 rebounds, 3.3 assists and 1.0 steals. He underwent surgery in May to address left shoulder instability.

And the Hornets are ecstatic about Knueppel, the fourth pick in last year's draft who led the league in 3-pointers made as a rookie. Knueppel averaged 18.5 points and 5.3 rebounds while shooting 42.5% from 3.

"Historic rookie season, I'd argue he should have been rookie of the year," Peterson said. "But the thing about Kon is he truly doesn't care about that stuff. He just wants to continue to maximize himself and ultimately do whatever he needs to do to get better and help us achieve the results that we want to achieve."

The Hornets also expect Coby White to help fill the void left at point guard by Ball's departure. The 6-foot-4 guard, who signed a three-year, $74 million deal to return, averaged 15.6 points and shot 39% from 3 in 21 games for Charlotte after being traded from Chicago.

"When we first traded for Coby, the priority was to always keep him and that was with [or] without LaMelo," Peterson said. "... I don't want to sit here and compare Coby White to LaMelo, but look: Coby's proven that he can be a very, very impactful player in this league. He did it in Chicago. He obviously hit a huge shot for us in the play-in game against Miami. But aside from the shotmaking, I do believe he's an underrated passer. He can push the pace." -- Ohm Youngmisuk

McMenamin: Lakers' Thiero impressing in summer league

Left knee surgery following his junior season at Arkansas caused Los Angeles Lakers second-year forward Adou Thiero to miss the NBA draft combine, and he never went through the physical tests and measurements to see just how much talent is packed into his 6-foot-7, 220-pound frame.

After his strong showing in the Lakers' 96-84 win over the Oklahoma City Thunder on Friday -- when five of Thiero's eight field goals and 10 of his 20 points came on rim-rocking dunks -- he was asked if he knows how high he can jump.

"Still didn't test it," Thiero said with a smirk. "I know it's over 40 [inches], but I don't know. We still got to test it."

Recovering from surgery and other injury setbacks cost him a majority of his rookie campaign, but he finally got tested by coach JJ Redick in the playoffs and delivered with eight rebounds in 13 minutes in Game 3 of the second round against the Thunder.

The 22-year-old hopes to continue to be called on this coming season, with the L.A. roster undergoing major turnover so far this summer.

"Definitely feels good to go out and get the reps and then seeing some of the stuff you work on, you go out there and they work," Thiero said. "But, at the same time, it's still a lot of work to go."

While he's still unsure of his vertical leap, he had no doubt when asked who is the better dunker between him and Lakers rookie Cameron Carr, who had three dunks of his own Friday.

"I don't think Cam would want me to join him in the dunk contest," Thiero said. -- Dave McMenamin

Kram: Wilson impresses in summer league debut
The Chicago Bulls didn't draft Caleb Wilson at No. 4 because of his shooting. The 6-foot-9 forward made just seven total 3-pointers in 24 games at North Carolina last season, and he never attempted more than three in a single game.

But he looked every bit like an NBA marksman in his first summer league game, shooting 7-for-11 from distance in a dazzling display in a 97-96 loss to the Memphis Grizzlies in Las Vegas on Friday night. Wilson made catch-and-shoot 3s and pull-ups, contested step-backs and deep 3s from well beyond the arc. He almost made an eighth 3, which would have bested his entire total from last season, but had a foot on the line. He finished with 35 points on 12-of-21 shooting.

The broad rule of summer league is not to overreact to single-game shooting lines, which are subject to all sorts of small-sample flukiness. But Wilson's sheer willingness to attempt so many 3s -- and his confidence to keep pulling up from deep -- offers an intriguing look at how he might expand his game at the NBA level in his rookie year. -- Zach Kram

Golliver: How Dybantsa became the Wizards' No. 1 pick
Before AJ Dybantsa scored a head-to-head victory over Darryn Peterson in his Las Vegas summer league debut on Thursday, he beat out the University of Kansas product as the Washington Wizards' choice to be this year's top overall pick.

Washington, which held the No. 1 pick for the first time since 2010, landed on Dybantsa after a comprehensive evaluation process. As they weighed their options, the Wizards became enamored with Dybantsa's rare combination of size and scoring ability, his defensive versatility, his team-oriented personality and his exceptional performance in athletic testing, team sources said Friday.

The 6-foot-9 Dybantsa, who was the nation's leading scorer as a BYU freshman, showcased his attack-minded approach and comfort with the ball during his summer league debut. But the Wizards view him as a two-way prospect, one source said, because of his ability to "sit down" and defend point guards, wings and power forwards in space.

The Wizards are refashioning their team culture after five consecutive lottery trips, and they believe Dybantsa is a singular talent capable of inspiring fan excitement and meshing with veteran stars Trae Young and Anthony Davis. All of Washington's key veterans, including Young, Davis and Deandre Ayton, were on hand for Dybantsa's summer league debut, and the team reassembled for a news conference announcing Young's new contract extension Friday morning.

The Wizards have held lottery picks in each of the past five drafts, and one team source said Dybantsa had the most impressive testing results of any prospect it evaluated during that period. Washington was already drawn to Dybantsa because of his standout "eye test" evaluations in college, but it felt even more comfortable after reviewing his elite measurables.

Ultimately, the Wizards concluded Dybantsa was their man because he boasted superstar potential and lacked any "red or even yellow flags." -- Ben Golliver

Youngmisuk: Davis, Young in attendance for Dybantsa debut
Early in the LeBron James sweepstakes, there was speculation over whether he could end up in Golden State with the Warriors trading for his old teammate Anthony Davis.

On Thursday, though, Davis looked very much like a Washington Wizard. In the morning, he worked out at the Wizards' impressive practice facility at the Mandalay Bay. And later that night, Davis joined Trae Young in attendance for No. 1 pick AJ Dybantsa's debut as the Wizards opened Las Vegas Summer League against No. 2 pick Darryn Peterson and the Utah Jazz.

It was a momentous night for the franchise, with team owner Ted Leonsis sitting courtside beside general manager Will Dawkins. The two were visited by John Wall, Washington's pick at No. 1 in 2010, who also came to watch Dybantsa's debut.

And in keeping with the positive vibes around the franchise, Davis walked onto the team's practice court earlier in the morning for a workout in a sleeveless Wizards hoodie and team shorts, looking healthy and in great shape.

Davis is eligible for a contract extension that he can sign for up to four years and $275 million starting Aug. 6. The first year of the extension would replace a $62.8 million player option for 2027-28.

Although Golden State is pursuing James and Davis had been linked to the Warriors as a way to potentially lure James to the Warriors to play with his former Lakers big man, Davis looked awfully comfortable as a Wizard here in Las Vegas on Thursday.

After Dybantsa scored 27 points to help Washington beat Utah, Davis walked off the floor with Patrick Ewing, a new Wizards assistant coach and Hall of Fame big man, right behind him. They looked like a formidable Washington tandem. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

McMenamin: Heat rookie Conwell impresses at California Classic

Miami Heat rookie guard Ryan Conwell.

"He's been killing," Carr said after Lakers practice in Las Vegas on Thursday. "He's been doing his thing."

The 6-foot-4 lefty out of Louisville averaged 21.0 points, 5.0 rebounds and 3.3 assists in his three games in the California Classic.

Miami acquired Conwell on draft night, sending cash considerations to the Oklahoma City Thunder in the deal after they selected him with the No. 37 pick.

As the Heat look to fill out the roster with shooting around Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo, Conwell could be a key cost-efficient addition after inking a three-year deal that will pay him $1.3 million next season. -- Dave McMenamin

Warriors keeping roster spot open for LeBron
The Golden State Warriors enter the second week of July yet to sign an outside free agent.

They were among the group of teams registering a level of interest in veteran wing Rui Hachimura and scoring guard Anfernee Simons, league sources said, but didn't meet the ultimate price point for a contract on either.

Simons went off the board to the Philadelphia 76ers for two years and $12.3 million -- nearly the same contract the Warriors gave to De'Anthony Melton.

They opted to retain Melton instead of putting more behind a pursuit of Simons, team sources said, because of a belief that Melton better fits the backcourt needs of the healthiest version of their current roster. He's not as explosive a scorer but is a more versatile and effective perimeter defender and pairs well with Stephen Curry.

Hachimura's contract terms (two years, $28 million to the LA Clippers) also came in higher than the Warriors proved willing to stretch. They have limited financial flexibility after bringing back Al Horford and Kristaps Porzingis, keeping space for Draymond Green to ultimately return and continuing their slow pursuit of LeBron James.

On the James front, Warriors sources continue to express a low level of optimism that James will ultimately pick them as his next team, but they intend to keep roster space open for James until he ultimately declares his choice. -- Anthony Slater

Expect Monday to be the busiest day on the NBA calendar
Starting at 12:01 p.m. ET, the moratorium will be lifted, meaning the trades that are sending Giannis Antetokounmpo to Miami, Jaylen Brown to Philadelphia, Kawhi Leonard to Toronto and LaMelo Ball to Minnesota can be finalized.

The timeline of trade calls is comparable to waiting on the runway for takeoff. Each trade has a designated time slot for its call, starting early in the afternoon and lasting into the evening. Keep in mind however that players involved in trades must report and pass a physical for a trade to become official.

Trades are not the only transaction that can become official. All player contracts negotiated and agreed upon can be finalized. For example, the Hornets can officially ink Coby White to the three-year, $74 million contract that had been reported.

Teams are also allowed to begin signing players that are extension-eligible. The list of notable players eligible on Monday include Nikola Jokic, Karl-Anthony Towns, Victor Wembanyama, Amen and Ausar Thompson and Cason Wallace. Donovan Mitchell is eligible starting Tuesday.

One more item to watch is restricted free agents, notably Peyton Watson and Jalen Duren.

If either player signs an offer sheet prior to noon ET, his prior team will have until 11:59 p.m. ET on July 7 to match. If the offer sheet comes in after noon ET, his prior team has until 1:59 p.m. ET on July 8 to match. -- Bobby Marks

Why Dolan is so worried about the second apron
The New York Knicks' championship parade has not even started, but there are already questions over whether finances will break up the roster.

"If we could bring back the whole team, exactly as is, why wouldn't you?" Knicks owner James Dolan said Wednesday on WFAN's "Carton Show." "I don't know if we'll be able to.

"We're willing to stretch, but there's certain things in the NBA that you'd have to be suicidal to do. One of them is the second apron. Cannot go into the second apron."

Including the 24th pick in next week's draft (June 23 and 24, 8 p.m. ET on ABC/ESPN), New York is $13 million below the second apron and has decisions with free agents Landry Shamet, Mitchell Robinson and possibly Jose Alvarado. (Alvarado has until Monday to decide on his $4.5 million option.) The entire starting five, meanwhile, is under contract through at least 2026-27. Karl-Anthony Towns is extension-eligible this summer and can become a free agent in the 2027 offseason if an agreement is not reached.

The second apron is a punitive luxury tax threshold restricting how teams add to their rosters in free agency, trades and the draft. In the case of the Knicks, the team would not be allowed to send cash in a trade, use the $6.1 million tax midlevel exception, aggregate salaries in a trade or use more than 100% of the traded player exception.

A team cannot trade its first-round pick seven years out if it finishes over the second apron in consecutive seasons, which no team has ever done. That same pick could be moved back to the end of the first round if a team finishes over the second apron in three out of four seasons. Luckily for Dolan and the Knicks, there are no rules that prohibit a team from retaining its own players.

New York can exceed the threshold to sign Robinson, Shamet and Alvarado. If the Knicks let the three players sign elsewhere, they would have their first-round pick (New York also has the 31st and 55th picks in the second round), the $6.1 million tax midlevel exception and $2.5 million veteran minimum exceptions available as replacements.

Since the apron rules were implemented before the 2024-25 season, Cleveland, Phoenix, Minnesota and Boston have finished the regular season over the second apron. The Knicks finished the past two seasons $53,000 and $370,000 below. Next offseason, New York is projected to be $31 million below the second apron with seven players under contract. -- Bobby Marks

The Minnesota Timberwolves won the battle on Saturday night, with a stirring Game 4 victory over Denver that brought the team within a win of the second round.

The Timberwolves rely on a strong core, with little depth behind it; entering Saturday's games, only seven Wolves had averaged more than 10 minutes per game in the playoffs. Why LaMelo's flagrant 2 falls into a gray area
The NBA retroactively assessed Charlotte Hornets guard LaMelo Ball with a flagrant foul 2 for tripping Miami Heat center Bam Adebayo in Tuesday's Eastern Conference play-in game, which Charlotte won in overtime thanks to Ball's last-second layup.

But for the Heat and their fans, it doesn't erase Adebayo's injury, it doesn't remove Ball from Friday's 8-9 game against the Orlando Magic and it all but certainly won't impact the Hornets should they reach the first round.

That's because one quirk of the tournament's addition is that, not unlike the NBA Cup title game, the play-in tournament lives as its own statistical entity. They are neither playoff nor regular-season games, with no bearing on postseason and regular-season stats or awards.

That's also the case with flagrant foul points, which can have a massive impact when they start to add up. In 2016, Draymond Green was suspended for Game 5 of the NBA Finals for accumulating four flagrant points over the course of the postseason, something that helped Cleveland pull off its stunning 3-1 comeback.

While the Hornets' playoff stay isn't likely to last as long -- Charlotte needs to win Friday just to set up a first-round meeting with the top-seeded Detroit Pistons -- Ball entering the playoffs with two flagrant points would have at least given heft to the belated punishment.

Instead, the decision felt fairly hollow. And in asking sources around the league Wednesday ahead of the NBA's announcement that Ball wouldn't be suspended, opinions were mixed. Some argued that a hefty fine would suffice, because you shouldn't retroactively remove him from the next game because of Adebayo's unfortunate injury. Others argued the opposite, saying he should have to sit out Friday's win-and-in showdown.

None of it, however, will reverse the agonizing end to Miami's season.

"I'm not really thinking about that anymore," Heat coach Erik Spoelstra told reporters Thursday during the team's exit interviews. "I don't think [Ball] is a dirty player. It should have been caught in the moment, and it wasn't. And you move on." -- Tim Bontemps

The NBA's take on tanking

ESPN's Anthony Slater talked to players, coaches and executives about how they feel about tanking in the NBA and the future it has in the league.

In ESPN's conversations with dozens of players, coaches and front office executives, a consistent theme emerged: Nobody likes it -- "I hate it," Golden State Warriors coach Steve Kerr said -- but not many deny it is often the most prudent team-building path when stuck near the bottom. Different seasons and different drafts will generate different forms, but everyone agrees it'll continue until the NBA figures out either the proper rules or punishments to curb it.

"These teams are doing the whole gamut: sitting guys in the fourth, playing analytically bad lineups, drawing up plays for bad shots," one Western Conference general manager said. "The creativity is impressive and I don't blame them. It's the best strategy to get better. Look at all the most promising teams in the league: Thunder, Spurs, Pistons, Rockets, Hornets. Years of being bad and building up on high picks. It's painful but worthwhile."

The strategies are growing in audaciousness and frequency of use. The orders from management are coming in earlier in the season, creating months of competitively compromised and often unwatchable basketball. The average margin of victory in NBA games this season is 13.1 points, the largest spread in history, and a record 89 games have been decided by 30 or more points.

"I think this draft is, in some ways, similar to the [2024 Zaccharie] Risacher year, but on a higher level," they said. "That year it was like, 'Is anyone going to be really good?' This year, it's like, 'Well, s---, there's a lot of guys.' You have high confidence that at least some of them are going to be really, really good. You're not really sure which ones.
"You don't want to be drafting at 1 and end up with the fifth-best player."

The NBA draft lottery takes place on May 10 ahead of the draft on June 25 and 26.

What scouts, execs are watching in top five picks

March 31

What's next for LeBron this offseason?
ESPN's Tim Bontemps and Dave McMenamin broke down the six possible avenues LeBron James could take this offseason, including staying with the Los Angeles Lakers, returning home to Cleveland and or landing with some surprising wildcard teams around the league.

Next for LeBron? NBA insiders on Lakers, Cavs, free agency options

March 27

How scouts and front offices view the Spurs' playoff chances
In their weekly intel file, ESPN's Tim Bontemps and Brian Windhorst talked to coaches, front offices and scouts to gauge the growing hype around the San Antonio Spurs' playoff run.

"They're my favorite now," the scout told ESPN. "I've been thinking a lot about it. His game is going to be even more dominant in the playoffs and every game he's going to get more and more into your head. In Game 1, your players will think about him on some of their shots. By Game 4, they'll be having full-on nightmares."
The Spurs are currently two games behind the Oklahoma City Thunder for the top seed in the Western Conference.

stories.headline: Fantasy hockey sleepers and busts: Players to draft or avoid at current draft spot
stories.summary: Who are the players going too high, or too low, compared to their expected fantasy hockey production?
stories.body:
Overachievers. In fantasy competition, to identify and secure them is to love them. There's no better complement to our unsurprising stars and other reliable contributors than a player (or more) who blows our too-modest preseason expectations right out of the rink. Whether of the breakout, bounce-back, or other variety, sleepers -- grabbed in late stages of a draft or even once play is underway -- go a long way in helping any competitive manager contend for a championship.

For this exercise, we're focusing on skaters who have been around the block a bit, as opposed to rookies or other breakout candidates like Jimmy Snuggerud, Jackson Blake, and Will Smith. We're tackling those similarly coveted fantasy performers elsewhere in our department. Also, you might notice a trend of fresh faces in new places applying to many of the following sleeper candidates. That's no coincidence. These potentially underrated fantasy skaters were not only actively pursued by their new teams, but acquired to fill a prominent position, which offers them an improved opportunity to make a bigger splash than otherwise.

Of course, you also want to avoid using too high of a draft pick in selecting players belonging on the other end of the meeting-expectations spectrum. So we're also including a few possible busts to steer clear of overly early on.

Ranking position provided by the preseason top 250, as of Sept. 16. N/A means the player currently ranks below that mark.

More: Sign up for free | Rankings | Projections | League types

Sleepers

Patrick Kane, F, Chicago Blackhawks (RW30)

They don't call him "Showtime" for nothing. Mark it, the 37-year-old is going to put on a sparkling display in his return to Chicago. If healthy enough, Kane's going to produce. It's as simple as that. The future Hall-of-Famer hasn't averaged more than a point/game for his 19-year career by happenstance. As for the winger's current physical condition, according to the Chicago Sun-Times, head coach Jeff Blashill believes his veteran star is feeling fit.

"He feels as good as he has in a long time. He's skating well, he's moving well," Blashill said. "Guys that play with their brain first seem to last a long time in this league, and he certainly has."

Then consider the eventual top-line and power-play assignment alongside burgeoning superstar Connor Bedard, who's due to return from a shoulder injury in early November. (Kane will make do well enough with gifted rookie center Anton Frondell or whoever else in the meanwhile.) All promising stuff. If the vet can carve out upwards of 70 games this campaign, he's well worth rostering in most leagues.

Mats Zuccarello, F, Los Angeles Kings (RW36)

Sure, he'll miss playing with winger Kirill Kaprizov in Minnesota. Who wouldn't? But there are much worse fates than landing on a top unit and power play with Artemi Panarin. Perennially underrated as a fantasy asset, all Zuccarello does is produce regularly. Averaging 0.92 points/game this past season, the 39-year-old is hardly slowing down with age. Durability remains the only concern here, as the veteran hasn't banged out anything near a complete season since 2022-23. But that's why you have IR spots. Draft Zuccarello late as a potential gem in his new Los Angeles digs.

Valeri Nichushkin, F, Columbus Blue Jackets (LW24)

When healthy and active -- admittedly an issue over the years in Dallas and Colorado -- the power forward is capable of putting up fantasy numbers with the best of them. He shoots, hits, scores and contributes frequently on the power play. After a modest year by his standards, the ex-Avalanche is now set to enjoy a fresh start as a more prominent player in Columbus. No longer in the company of Nathan MacKinnon, Martin Necas, Gabriel Landeskog and others, Nichushkin can sink his teeth into a larger role on a top line and power play with Jackets star and countryman Kirill Marchenko. The 31-year-old played 72 contests this past regular season, more than he has in a long while. At his best, Nichushkin is capable of averaging 2.0 points/game in ESPN standard leagues.

Gabriel Landeskog, F, Colorado Avalanche (N/A)

Ranking-wise, MacKinnon is cream of the fantasy crop in ESPN standard competition. Reasonably enough, Necas sits several notches below at 31st overall. Then we need to scroll all the way down to realize Landeskog isn't even included in the top 250. Bit odd, considering the Avalanche captain is slated to play with the aforementioned pair on Colorado's top line and power play. Or that he collected 11 points in 13 playoff games after his first full-ish season following what essentially amounted to a three-year absence from the game. Healthy and fit, which he is now, the still-only 33-year-old is capable of putting up 70 points alongside MacKinnon and Necas. No question, he's worth grabbing in deeper leagues.

ESPN Fantasy Hockey is the fun, free way to get inside the game. Draft your players, set your lineups and earn points when the pros do. Sign up today!

Mason Marchment, F, San Jose Sharks (N/A)

After showing flashes of potential in Florida and Dallas and Seattle and Columbus, the too-well traveled veteran now gets to play with Macklin Celebrini in San Jose. If he manages to keep a grip on that assignment, the 31-year-old is going to score 30 goals and 35-plus assists this season. A gig on San Jose's top power play, again alongside Celebrini, isn't out of the question either.

Jiri Kulich, F, Buffalo Sabres (N/A)

More specifically qualifying as a breakout candidate, Kulich still very comfortably fits the broader "sleeper" mold heading into 2026-27. After suffering a devastating -- and potentially career-ending -- blood clot last November, the 22-year-old underwent successful surgery and is ready to resume play. Selected 28th overall in 2022, he's expected to be offered the ripe opportunity to make a profound impression on a top line with Tage Thompson and fellow breakout candidate Zach Benson. If that's how it indeed shakes out in Buffalo, draft Kulich late in deeper leagues or off the wire before regular play gets underway. Before your fellow managers become more familiar with the kid who scored 15 goals in 62 games as a rookie two years ago.

Adam Fox, D, New York Rangers (D27)

D27? So we should draft 26 other NHL defenders before the guy who won the Norris five years ago? Who, at 28 years old, still enjoys top-pair minutes and competes on New York's No. 1 power play? That guy? I get that Fox may have fallen off some fantasy radars after losing a chunk of time to injury last season, but he still collected 53 points, including 24 with the extra skater, in 55 games. And the top-15 fantasy defenseman is once again healthy.

Stuart Skinner, G, Winnipeg Jets (G32)

So now camp no-show Connor Hellebuyck is suspended by the Jets. Hmm. Does this action further inspire management and hasten the goalie's exit out of Winnipeg, or do matters become even messier? Regardless, Skinner remains in place and is revving to go. The recent two-time Stanley Cup Finalist is presently the undisputed No. 1 for a solid-enough Jets team that's ready to put last year's debacle behind it. While this situation remains fluid -- GM Kevin Cheveldayoff could/should acquire a quality netminder as part of a package in return for Hellebuyck -- Skinner is still worth a flyer in all but the shallowest of fantasy leagues.

See also:

Seth Jones, D, Florida Panthers (N/A)
Jacob Markstrom , G, Florida Panthers (G30)

Made it this far? Create your own league with your own rules and play against your friends today.

Busts

Steven Stamkos, F, Nashville Predators (C14)

He isn't likely to score 40-plus again this season. According to Evolving Hockey, Stamkos should have netted approximately 34 goals (34.33 ixG) in 2025-26, not 42. His unsustainable 20.4% shooting percentage supports such evaluation. Projected to average around 17 minutes/game on Nashville's second line and the top power play, Stamkos sports a realistic ceiling of 30-35 goals and 25 assists, with a solid number of points counting with the man-advantage. Decent numbers indeed, but not near top-30. There are about 25 other NHL forwards who I would draft before the 36-year-old veteran.

Alex Ovechkin, F, Washington Capitals (LW11)

It's all relative, right? As a fantasy performer, this isn't your mother's Ovechkin. At 41 years old, the greatest goal-scorer of all time is back for another kick at the Stanley Cup can. If contributions from supporting castmates, including a host of newbies like Alex Tuch, Jordan Kyrou and Boone Jenner, help him get there, personal stats be darned. Sure, he'll flirt with 30 goals on a pile of shots in a full, healthy season (tougher ask this round with no elongated Olympic break), and many of them will count on the power play. But, again, there are too many other options around the league with greater fantasy potential. Especially if Ovechkin drops down the Caps lineup, as anticipated.

Morgan Geekie, F, Boston Bruins (C34)

Receiving positive attention in this space as a sleeper candidate last season, the Bruins winger didn't disappoint those willing to take the early plunge. At least until Christmas. Less notably, after scoring 25 goals in his first 36 games, Geekie only managed another 14 in his final 45. Which leaves us less optimistic about the 28-year-old's prospects this campaign, even if he remains on David Pastrnak's wing.

Brent Burns, D, Colorado Avalanche (D45)

Unless your preferred team is facing him in the Final, who wouldn't want to see Burns hoist the Stanley Cup? We all love the 41-year-old defender. But his finest fantasy days are behind him. Pegged to play on the third pair in Colorado and unlikely to enjoy any significant time with the extra skater, Burns projects to put up 30 or so even-strength points and not enough blocked shots to compensate otherwise. According to Evolving Hockey, he was supposed to score only six goals (6.62 ixG), yet he potted 12. The fourth-ranked fantasy defender on his own team behind Cale Makar, Devon Toews and Sam Malinski, Burns should only be rostered in deeper ESPN conventional leagues. His durability isn't enough.

Dan Vladar, G, Philadelphia Flyers (G18)

Joseph Woll is a good goalie. Better than Samuel Ersson. If the former Maple Leaf remains healthy, he'll eat into Vladar's playing time. Then there's the incumbent's small sample size. As impressed as we all are with how the ex-Flame conducted himself in his first year as Philly's go-to, it was just the one season. Plus, are the Flyers a playoff team again? In the Metropolitan Division, the Capitals are better, no one would be surprised to see the Devils and Rangers improve on their respective records, and Carolina remains Carolina. There's another crowd of netminders I'm chasing before Vladar as my second fantasy goalie in deeper leagues.

See also:

John Gibson, G, Detroit Red Wings (G16)

stories.headline: UFC 331 preview and picks: Pantoja sees opportunity in disaster
stories.summary: Top storylines and coaches' analysis for UFC 331 in Los Angeles.
stories.body:
For two and a half years, Alexandre Pantoja ruled the UFC's flyweight division at a level unseen since the historic era of Demetrious Johnson nearly 10 years ago. And yet, the past nine months since his last fight could prove to be the most compelling of Pantoja's career.
The 36-year-old Pantoja (30-6) will challenge Joshua Van (17-2) for the 125-pound championship at UFC 331 inside Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles on Saturday. It will be his first appearance since UFC 323 in December, when he lost the belt to Van via TKO after Pantoja suffered a dislocated elbow 26 seconds into the fight. The nature of the loss has led to a feeling of unfinished business between the two fighters going into Saturday's main event.

"As an athlete, yes, I have a TKO loss on my record," Pantoja told ESPN. "I've never lost by TKO or submission before. Nobody had ever finished me. Now, I have that. But personally, as a man? No. I don't believe I have a loss to him."

Pantoja won the title against Brandon Moreno in 2023 and defended the belt four times before meeting Van. He was among the best pound-for-pound fighters in the world at the time. But with a comeback narrative attached to him for this fight, he said there is an added level of excitement.

"For sure, this is an opportunity," Pantoja said. "In my soul, that's the opportunity. Now, I get to fight the champion. He's the champion of the world and I love that. It makes the fight more spicy for me."

Van, 24, has embraced the narrative -- even while cementing himself as the undisputed champion. There are those who say Van needs to defeat Pantoja again to legitimize his championship, but Van's first title defense against Tatsuro Taira in May made discrediting him harder. Taira's ground game posed a real threat to Van, but he ultimately knocked out the Japanese challenger in the fifth round of a matchup that earned fight of the night honors at UFC 328.

The unfinished business, Pantoja's return and Van's undeniable star power mean Saturday's flyweight title fight is shaping up to be the most anticipated 125-pound title fight since Henry Cejudo ended Johnson's nearly five-year title reign in 2018 then defended the flyweight belt against then-bantamweight champion TJ Dillashaw in 2019.

For Pantoja specifically, his worst stroke of bad luck could turn into the greatest night of his career.

"Saturday night is going to be my best night, man," Pantoja said. "I haven't been to work in 10 months. That's why all of these fights, and this one especially, is worth so much. We work for months to just get one night of work. I've recovered my arm. Now I have an opportunity to show everyone what I did in the last 10 months."

More storylines to watch
History isn't in Pantoja's favor
If Alexandre Pantoja is searching for role models to inspire this weekend's quest to reclaim the championship he lost suddenly and painfully last December, he would be wise to look beyond recent history.

Within the past two weeks, two of the UFC's 11 champs -- women's flyweight Valentina Shevchenko and heavyweight Tom Aspinall -- vacated their titles because of health issues. Their paths back to the top of the mountain are as yet uncharted.

Before them, the most recent champions to lose their titles to injuries did not fare well upon their returns. In November 2022, Jiří Procházka vacated the UFC light heavyweight title after hurting his shoulder in training. His successor was Jamahal Hill, who just months after winning the vacant title had to vacate it himself after rupturing an Achilles. As soon as he was healed, Hill was granted an opportunity to reclaim his title and lost. Procházka was given three shots at the 205-pound belt and fell short in all of them.

For a success story, Pantoja must look deeper into UFC championship history to the brutal health issues overcome by Dominick Cruz. While preparing for a bantamweight title defense in May 2012, Cruz tore the anterior cruciate ligament in his left knee. He underwent surgery, then had a setback requiring a second ACL surgery six months later. He was scheduled to return in February 2014 but suffered a groin tear in training. Facing another extended recovery, he vacated his title.

Cruz returned that September and won a fight that put him in position for a shot at his old belt. Three months later, he tore his other ACL.

Finally, in February 2016 -- more than four years after his last title fight -- Cruz challenged TJ Dillashaw for the belt and won a split decision. "I had to show something to myself," Cruz said afterward. "That's what this was."

Tsarukyan's chance to set things right again
Arman Tsarukyan was labeled a snubbed man after it was announced that Justin Gaethje and Paddy Pimblett would headline the first UFC card of 2026 with the No. 1 lightweight contender status at stake. It's hard to remember that sentiment now, considering the year Tsarukyan has had.

In the absence of an obvious UFC fight to take, Tsarukyan has wrestled competitively -- mostly in RAF -- 10 times in 2026. He raised his social media presence exponentially behind videos of lavish cars, extraordinary meals and collaborations with content creator Nina Drama. This is the longest layoff of his UFC career, but his brand has grown more during that time off than from any single fight.

He appears in a good position to get back to work and finally earn the title shot many have said he should have already had. But it won't be an easy fight. Tsarukyan's opponent, Mauricio Ruffy, is a dangerous underdog (+270, according to DraftKings). This fight will restore the order the top of the 155-pound division has lacked in Tsarukyan's absence, regardless of who wins.

Another step for Steveson?

Any MMA prospect would almost certainly switch places with 26-year-old UFC newcomer Gable Steveson. When you're an Olympic gold medal wrestler, and one of the most touted heavyweight prospects in MMA history, certain opportunities are going to come to you that others aren't afforded. It also means Steveson's window for error is small, as he's asked to learn and develop under the sport's brightest lights.

The UFC is managing his opposition. For his second UFC appearance (and fifth pro fight overall), he'll take on Sean Sharaf, a 33-year-old with two knockout losses in his first two UFC fights. Steveson will once again be a heavy, heavy favorite (-2100 by DraftKings), as he was for his promotional debut in July. The heavyweight division is wide open now that Tom Aspinall has vacated his title and the list of top contenders is thin, so Steveson's performance probably means more than the result. If he continues to look the part, his career trajectory could be accelerated at a rate few see.

Coaches' questions and predictions
"Can Pantoja bank enough rounds on the ground, while staying responsible on the feet?"

What a fight this will be. Van shows up in big moments; he's just a proven gamer. If Pantoja stands with Van, he's going to get hurt. Pantoja is good at applying pressure and landing the 1-2 punch (lead left jab, right cross), but he cannot play that game with Van, because of Van's counterboxing. Van's hands are too fast. Van can land four-to-six shots at a time in close distance, and that's something Pantoja really has to watch for. Van is going to have confidence in his ability to get off the ground from his last fight against Taira. I'm going to stay on the fence and say it's a pick 'em. After watching Van's fight with Taira, though, knowing how good Taira is on the ground, it's a little unfair to say Van can't weather the storm on the ground with Pantoja. -- Sayif Saud, Fortis MMA

Prediction: Too close to call

"How big of a setback is Pantoja's injury at age 36?"
Van is young, fired up and he's got bricks in his hands. We've seen some small weaknesses in his game, which are obviously due to lack of experience. He's getting better all the time. If Pantoja comes back and is anywhere close to where he was when he was holding the belt, I think he gets it back. There are just too many variables on the ground. We saw Van get mounted by Taira. Van is going to go to work on fixing that hole in his game, but Pantoja is so good. The biggest question is how bad of a setback is Pantoja's injury, at this stage of his career? He's not a spring chicken. But if he's the same Pantoja, he gets the win, potentially by submission. -- John Wood, Syndicate MMA

Prediction: Pantoja by decision or submission

"Can Ruffy stop takedowns and keep space?"

Arman has been on such a tear with the wrestling in RAF, showing his ability to wrestle bigger guys and show his power and skill in grappling. When it comes to that, he is very dangerous. Ruffy is finding his groove, and he's very sharp on the feet, but former opponents King Green and Michael Chandler don't pose the same grappling threat that Arman poses. I think Benoît Saint Denis kind of exposed that hole in Ruffy's game. It's not to say Ruffy doesn't have a chance. In space, he is a problem. He can absolutely starch Arman in space. But how does he keep a powerhouse like Arman at distance? -- Saud

Prediction: Tsarukyan by decision

"Has Ruffy improved his ground defense enough?"
This is a really interesting fight. Arman is going to want to grind out Ruffy. Arman is easily a top-five wrestler/grappler in the UFC. The one thing about Arman -- even though he's stayed busy with the wrestling appearances, he's been out of the UFC for a while, so it'll be interesting to see how he looks. But unless Ruffy catches him and knocks him out, Arman is a good striker, too. Arman can go the distance in a hard fight. My gut leans to Arman. I'm a big fan of Ruffy, but it's just that grappling prowess of Arman. -- Wood

Prediction: Tsarukyan by decision

ESPN's Jeff Wagenheim contributed to this story.

stories.headline: Lewis Hamilton shuts down asking Ferrari to make changes: 'Never asked for anyone to be replaced'
stories.summary: Lewis Hamilton denied he has called for replacements at Ferrari after he admitted his bid for a record eight world championship is over.
stories.body:
Lewis Hamilton denied he has called for replacements at Ferrari after he admitted his bid for a record eighth world championship is over.

Hamilton threw in the title towel at last weekend's Spanish Grand Prix after he retired from the race in Madrid with a brake problem.

His failure to finish leaves him 101 points behind Kimi Antonelli in the championship standings -- the equivalent of more than four victories -- with just nine scheduled rounds left.

A report in Italy claimed Hamilton has challenged Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur to make changes to the team's trackside staff.

But in a story posted to his Instagram account on Thursday, the 41-year-old wrote: "I've seen some of the stories that have gone out and I want to clear it up on here.

"I've never asked for anyone on my team to be replaced. Everyone I work with works hard every day, and their dedication is what moves us forward.

"I always try to empower and lift people to be the best versions of themselves or at least see the best in themselves.

"I may not always achieve that but it's my intention and what I'm here to do. We all work together and that will continue."

- Lando Norris backs 'exciting' 2027 Monaco GP sprint weekend but 'tougher for us drivers'

- Max vs 100: Verstappen jokes taking on '200' drivers next time after winning crazy challenge

- F1 2027 calendar: Monaco GP gets sprint race, Türkiye and Portugal return to schedule

Hamilton sparked hope of challenging Antonelli -- the driver who replaced him at Mercedes -- when he won in Barcelona in June.

However, the British driver has not finished on the podium at the past five rounds and has been openly critical of his team's race tactics.

He also took aim at teammate Charles Leclerc's driving after an opening-lap clash in Monza earlier this month. Hamilton said he led face-to-face talks with the Monegasque to clear the air.

His retirement in Madrid marked his first of the campaign, and when asked to assess his title chances, Hamilton replied: "There's no stopping him [Antonelli] and Mercedes this year. They've done a phenomenal job, and they deserve it [the championship]."

stories.headline: Borussia Dortmund teenager Konstantinos Karetsas returns to training after Champions League health scare
stories.summary: Borussia Dortmund says 18-year-old midfielder Konstantinos Karetsas is back in training just over a week after he slumped to the ground in an alarming medical incident on his Champions League debut.
stories.body:
Borussia Dortmund have said 18-year-old midfielder Konstantinos Karetsas is back in training just over a week after he slumped to the ground in an alarming medical incident on his Champions League debut.

Karetsas passed the ball to a teammate then signaled his distress to the referee before sitting on the grass during Dortmund's 3-2 win over Villarreal on Sept. 8.

He was in tears as he was stretchered off with suspected circulatory problems and was then taken to a hospital, where he stayed for much of last week.

"Konstantinos Karetsas is back in team training as of Wednesday after doing individual sessions at the start of the week," Dortmund said. "It was his first joint session with his teammates after he was taken off with circulatory problems in the game against Villarreal."

Dortmund hasn't specified the nature of any diagnosis for Karetsas, who was signed from Genk for a reported fee of $34.6 million last month, and didn't indicate whether he would be able to play Saturday against Stuttgart in the Bundesliga.

Karetsas plays internationally for Greece but was born in Belgium, where local media have reported that dehydration was suspected as a factor.

"I'm doing really well," he said in a video recorded during a visit to his old club Genk and published Monday on X. "We tested everything and everything is fine. I just need to adjust a bit to the intensity but that will come with time."

"I went out with him but in that moment, he wasn't able to speak," Book said.

- Borussia Dortmund teenager Karetsas hospitalised after slumping to turf in Champions League

Karetsas was able to cheer on his teammates from the stands in Saturday's 3-0 win over Paderborn.

Managing director Lars Ricken said there had been "no warning signs" of any circulatory problems prior to the incident.

stories.headline: 'It's all on': Fitzgibbon relishes Robbo coaching duel
stories.summary: Mates and mentors Craig Fitzgibbon and Trent Robinson have banned contact this week as the Cronulla and Sydney Roosters coaches chase an NRL preliminary final.
stories.body:
No more Mr Nice Guy, Craig Fitzgibbon has shoved friendship aside as he plots to shatter the Sydney Roosters' NRL title hopes for a second successive season.

After a decorated playing career with the Roosters, highlighted by his Clive Churchill-winning display in the Tricolours' 2002 premiership triumph, Fitzgibbon enjoyed a fruitful decade working under Trent Robinson as the club's assistant coach.

But that friendly relationship is on ice this week, with Fitzgibbon, wearing his Cronulla coaching hat, intent on ending the Roosters' season as the Sharks did last year with a 20-10 first-week ambush.

"It was a long time. I've had 10 years working with Trent, so it's definitely a long apprenticeship," Fitzgibbon said ahead of Saturday night's do-or-die battle at Allianz Stadium.

"I had plenty of lessons and am forever grateful for my time there and his mentoring of me to be a coach.

"And he was always supportive and backed me in to take the opportunity when that comes, so I'll be forever grateful for that.

"But this week is about Sharks versus Roosters and, whilst we talk regularly, we're not talking this week."

The latest episode in the pair's coaching rivalry will be the third time in the past four seasons that Cronulla and the Roosters clash in a sudden-death final, with Fitzgibbon and Robinson splitting the first two September showdowns.

The Roosters edged the Sharks 13-12 in 2023 before last year's loss.

Texting is taboo this week, with Fitzgibbon happy to wait until after fulltime to rekindle their great mateship.

"He's fine with that too," Fitzgibbon said.

"He's just as competitive as I am so, no, we'll shut it down this week. We've bumped into each other in plenty of semis now, so it's a contest and it's a game.

"A lot of work goes into a whole season, starting all the way back in the November before, so the ups and downs of the season.

"But you get to this end and it's all on."

Both sides fumbled and bumbled their way into this year's finals, the Sharks losing four of their last five regular-season games with star five-eighth Braydon Trindall sidelined with a dislocated shoulder.

After briefly sharing premiership favouritism after taking down Penrith in round 24, the Roosters also lost playmaker Sam Walker to an ankle injury during a run of four straight defeats.

While below the form that led the Sharks to nine wins from 10 starts before their slump, Fitzgibbon saw enough in last Saturday's 26-16 victory over North Queensland to be heartened.

"We played more like Sharks," he said.

"A bit more cohesion back in. Obviously there were some changes in and out and then we set on the line-up and got back to playing like we know we can.

"It was probably really physical early and we had to stay in the fight there for a bit and then managed to come out the other side and dealt with a couple of disallowed tries and dealt with a little bit of adversity to be able to not get flustered and stick to the plan."

Saturday night's victors will advance to a preliminary final against the Dolphins at Suncorp Stadium next Friday night.
